notes: Ruling monarchist slot 23 holds the Royal Lao Government under King Savang Vatthana and Prime Minister Souvanna Phouma; Souvanna's own Lao Neutralist Party sits in 13. Lao People's Party in 4 and Neo Lao Hak Sat in 5 follow MD (LPRP 4, its front's successor LFND 5). Vang Pao's CIA-backed SGU in 0, FAR in 22, House of Champassak in 14. Islamic slots are small immigrant communities.

0.name: Special Guerrilla Units
0.text:
The Special Guerrilla Units are the irregular army raised since 1961 by the CIA among the Hmong of northern Laos. Commanded by General Vang Pao from his secret base at Long Tieng in Military Region II, they bear the brunt of the war against the North Vietnamese and Pathet Lao on the Plain of Jars.

Vang Pao's forces are armed, paid and flown by the Americans and loyal above all to their commander. They seek the defeat of communism and security for the Hmong highlands, and their leverage lies in being the most effective fighting force on the royal side.

1.name: Phu Nyai Viangchan
1.text:
Phu Nyai Viangchan are the great families of the capital, above all the Sananikone clan, who fill the National Assembly, the ministries and the boards of trading companies. Former Prime Minister Phoui Sananikone remains their senior figure and a pillar of the royalist right.

They stand for the monarchy, Buddhism, private property and the American alliance, and distrust both the Pathet Lao and Souvanna's concessions to it. Their leverage lies in patronage, family ties to army commanders and control over the flow of American aid through Vientiane.

2.name: Lao Issara Kao
2.text:
Lao Issara Kao gathers veterans of the Free Lao movement that proclaimed independence from France in 1945 under Prince Phetsarath and later joined the royal government. Many now serve as officials, teachers and deputies in Vientiane and Luang Prabang.

They favour constitutional monarchy, an elected assembly with real powers, honest administration and national reconciliation between the royal government and the Pathet Lao. They resent both French nostalgia and American domination, and their leverage lies in their patriotic record and their bridges to both camps.

3.name: Khu Viangchan
3.text:
Khu Viangchan are the schoolteachers, junior civil servants and clerks of the capital, a small educated class squeezed by wartime inflation while generals and merchants grow rich. Underpaid and often trained in France or Thailand, they form the core of reformist opinion in Vientiane.

They demand fair wages, public schooling in Lao rather than French, land for refugees and an end to corruption, and want peace through a coalition with the Pathet Lao. Their leverage lies in their ability to strike and to mobilise students in the lycées of the capital.

4.name: Phak Pasason Lao
4.text:
The Lao People's Party was founded in secret in 1955 from the Lao section of the Indochinese Communist Party and is the hidden leadership behind the Pathet Lao. Its general secretary Kaysone Phomvihane directs the revolution from the caves of Sam Neua, in close partnership with Hanoi.

It aims to overthrow the monarchy and establish a people's democratic state on the Vietnamese model. Its strength lies in disciplined cadres, North Vietnamese troops and supplies, and control of the liberated zones along the Ho Chi Minh Trail.

5.name: Neo Lao Hak Sat
5.text:
The Neo Lao Hak Sat, the Lao Patriotic Front, was founded in 1956 as the political face of the Pathet Lao. Its chairman, Prince Souphanouvong, half-brother of Souvanna Phouma, withdrew from the coalition government in 1963 and leads the front from the liberated zone in Sam Neua.

It demands an end to American bombing and intervention, a new coalition government and land and dignity for the hill peoples. Its leverage lies in the guerrilla war, half the territory of the kingdom and the prestige of the 'Red Prince' among Lao nationalists.

6.name: Kong Phan Thi Song
6.text:
Kong Phan Thi Song are the veterans of Captain Kong Le's Second Paratroop Battalion, which seized Vientiane in August 1960 demanding an end to foreign interference and civil war. Kong Le himself has been in exile since 1966, but his officers and admirers remain in the neutralist units.

They are nationalist soldiers who resent the American advisers, Thai mercenaries and Vietnamese troops alike, and see Laos as a pawn of foreigners. Their leverage lies in disaffected officers, the legend of the 1960 coup and the memory of a soldier who defied every patron.

7.name: Kongthap Potpoi Pasason Lao
7.text:
The Lao People's Liberation Army is the armed force of the Pathet Lao, commanded by Khamtay Siphandone. It fights alongside North Vietnamese divisions on the Plain of Jars and along the Ho Chi Minh Trail, and controls the eastern and northern provinces.

It answers to the Lao People's Party, depends on Hanoi for weapons and advisers and denounces American bombing and the royal army as puppets. Its leverage lies in a hardened guerrilla force, the support of North Vietnam and the steady erosion of royal control in the countryside.

8.name: Khoja Jamat Viangchan
8.text:
Khoja Jamat Viangchan is the handful of Ismaili Khoja trading families from India and East Africa who run textile and import houses in Vientiane. They follow the Aga Khan, Prince Karim, whose modernising leadership stresses education, enterprise and loyalty to the host country.

They keep out of Lao politics, maintain friendly ties with the royal government and invest in schooling for their children. Their influence is limited to commerce, but their links with Bangkok, Bombay and Nairobi make them a small window on the wider Muslim world.

9.name: Bohra Jamaat Viangchan
9.text:
Bohra Jamaat Viangchan is the small community of Dawoodi Bohra traders in Vientiane, linked to the larger congregations of Bangkok and Saigon. They owe absolute obedience to their spiritual head, Syedna Mohammed Burhanuddin, who leads the Bohras from Bombay.

Their religious and commercial life is regulated by clergy appointed from Bombay, and they avoid any political engagement in Laos. Their leverage is purely economic, through hardware and import businesses and trading networks that stretch across Southeast Asia.

10.name: Pho Kha Islam Viangchan
10.text:
Pho Kha Islam Viangchan are the Sunni Muslim traders of the capital, mostly of Pakistani, Indian and Tamil origin, who keep shops and money-changing businesses around the central market. Their community life centres on prayer rooms and the hospitality of the Pakistani and Indonesian diplomats.

They are quietist and loyal to the royal government, which grants them residence and trading licences, and they avoid all politics. Their influence lies in commerce and currency exchange, which make them useful to Lao officials and foreign embassies alike.

11.name: Haw Islam
11.text:
Haw Islam are the Yunnanese Hui Muslim muleteers who have run armed caravans through the hills of northern Laos, Burma and Thailand for generations. Some families fled Yunnan after 1949 and now trade in salt, silver and opium in the Golden Triangle.

They recognise no government's authority over their caravans, defend their routes with their own rifles and are bitterly hostile to Chinese communism. Their leverage lies in mule trains, weapons and knowledge of the mountain paths that every army in the region needs.

12.name: Jamaat Viangchan
12.text:
Jamaat Viangchan is a small study group of Pakistani traders and clerks in Vientiane who read the works of Abul A'la Maududi, founder of the Jamaat-e-Islami in Lahore. They meet in private homes and collect funds for Islamic causes abroad.

They believe Muslims should organise politically to live under Islamic law and see communism as the main enemy of Islam. Their numbers are tiny, but their contacts with Pakistan and the wider Islamic movement give them a voice among Muslims scattered across Laos.

13.name: Phak Lao Pen Kang
13.text:
The Lao Neutralist Party was founded in 1961 by Prince Souvanna Phouma to organise the neutralist camp between the royalist right and the Pathet Lao. Since the Geneva Agreement of 1962 Souvanna has headed the government of national union, which now governs without the Pathet Lao ministers.

It seeks to keep Laos neutral under the 1962 agreement, preserve the monarchy and reopen talks with the Pathet Lao, while accepting American aid to survive. Its leverage lies in Souvanna's indispensability: he is the one figure accepted by Washington, Moscow and the Pathet Lao alike.

14.name: Na Champassak
14.text:
The House of Champassak ruled the southern Lao kingdom until 1946, when it renounced its throne in favour of unity under Luang Prabang. Its head, Prince Boun Oum na Champassak, former prime minister and Inspector General of the Kingdom, remains the leading figure of the south.

It stands for southern autonomy, royalism and staunch anti-communism, and has close ties with Thailand and the Americans. Its leverage lies in its estates, the loyalty of southern notables and the army commanders of the Mekong provinces, where Boun Oum's word carries more weight than Vientiane's.

15.name: Hang Kham Viangchan
15.text:
Hang Kham Viangchan are the Sino-Lao and Vietnamese trading houses that have made Vientiane a hub of the Asian gold trade, importing bullion legally and smuggling it into Thailand and South Vietnam. Their partners include generals and ministers who share in opium, timber and import licences.

They favour the war economy, American aid and a weak state that leaves trade untaxed, and fear any settlement that would empower the Pathet Lao. Their leverage lies in money that buys officers, deputies and votes in a capital awash with dollars.

16.name: Talat Sao
16.text:
Talat Sao takes its name from Vientiane's Morning Market, where Lao, Chinese and Vietnamese shopkeepers, money-changers and small importers trade everything from Thai rice to American transistor radios. They are the small business class that has grown with the aid economy.

They want low taxes, free trade with Thailand and protection from extortion by officials and soldiers, and see the Pathet Lao as a threat to private property. Their leverage lies in controlling the everyday supply of the capital and in the political goodwill that cheap goods buy.

17.name: Phra Pa
17.text:
Phra Pa are the forest-dwelling monks of the meditation tradition who live in remote hermitages along the Mekong and in the southern hills. Villagers revere them as guardians of the sacred forests where cutting trees and hunting are forbidden.

They teach that the forest, its animals and its spirits must be protected, and quietly oppose the logging concessions granted to generals and the devastation of the bombed countryside. Their leverage lies in the deep respect of rural Lao for monks and in the moral weight of the Sangha.

18.name: Kamlang Pen Kang Hak Sat
18.text:
The Patriotic Neutralist Forces broke away from Kong Le's neutralist army in 1963 under Colonel Deuane Sounnarath and allied with the Pathet Lao. They hold positions in Xieng Khouang and around the Plain of Jars and claim to be the true heirs of the 1960 neutralist revolution.

They call for a genuinely neutral Laos, the withdrawal of American forces and a coalition government including the Neo Lao Hak Sat, combined with social reforms. Their leverage lies in giving the Pathet Lao a non-communist ally and a bridge to Souvanna's own camp.

19.name: Nak Hian Lao Paris
19.text:
Nak Hian Lao Paris are the Lao students in France, sons and daughters of the Vientiane elite sent abroad on government scholarships. Radicalised by May 1968 and the Vietnam War, many have turned to Marxism and read Mao alongside Sartre.

They denounce the royal government as an American puppet and sympathise with the Pathet Lao, but some prefer an independent, Chinese-inspired revolution to Hanoi's tutelage. Their leverage lies in the future: they are the educated cadres both sides will need when they return home.

20.name: Sai Phoumi
20.text:
Sai Phoumi are the followers of General Phoumi Nosavan, once the strongman of the American-backed right, who fled to Thailand after his failed coup of February 1965. From Bangkok he keeps in touch with officers and politicians who still hope for his return.

They want a hard line against the Pathet Lao and North Vietnam, an end to neutralist compromises and a strong nationalist government backed by the army. Their leverage lies in Phoumi's Thai connections and in rightist officers frustrated with Souvanna's leadership.

21.name: Auto-Défense de Choc
21.text:
The Auto-Défense de Choc are the armed village militias raised by the royal government and its American advisers to hold villages against the Pathet Lao. Lightly armed and poorly paid, they guard roads, refugee settlements and hill villages across the kingdom.

They are fiercely anti-communist and often answer to local strongmen rather than Vientiane, punishing suspected sympathisers without trial. Their leverage lies in their numbers and their presence in places where the regular army never goes.

22.name: Forces Armées Royales
22.text:
The Royal Lao Armed Forces are the regular army of the kingdom, commanded by General Ouane Rattikone and divided into five military regions whose commanders, such as General Kouprasith Abhay in Vientiane, act as regional powers. Financed and supplied by the United States, it fights alongside American air power.

Its officer corps is royalist and anti-communist but riven by rivalries, profiteering and coups. Its leverage lies in its weapons, its control of the Mekong towns and the willingness of its generals to decide who governs in Vientiane.

23.name: Latthaban Latsa-anachak Lao
23.text:
The Royal Lao Government rules the Kingdom of Laos in the name of King Savang Vatthana, who has reigned from Luang Prabang since 1959. Prince Souvanna Phouma heads it as prime minister of the government of national union formed in 1962, now reduced to royalists and neutralists.

It stands for the throne, Buddhism and the 1962 neutrality agreement, while relying on American aid and air power to survive. Its leverage lies in the King's sacred authority, international recognition and control of the Mekong valley where most Lao live.
